parts:
Dear Professors,

I ask to forgive for my English language, and I hope you understand me.
In using a replication example I was wanting to be certain about my solutions and compare the results from both packages, by using the data called "d.partybans".

The complex solutions and the most parsiomonious solutions are the same, except for the intermediate solution that it is different and I don't know why.

I use this code:

library(QCApro)
data(d.partybans)
eQMC(d.partybans, outcome = "PB{1}", exo.facs = c("C", "F", "T", "V"), dir.exp = c(1, "1;2", 2, 1))

p.sol: C{0} + C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + T{2}*V{0}

M1:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*V{0}) => PB{1}
M2:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*T{0}) => PB{1}

p.sol: C{0} + C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + F{0}*T{2} + F{1}*V{0}

M1:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*V{0}) => PB{1}
M2:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*T{0}) => PB{1}


And then I compare this solutions with what I obtained from the other package QCA:

library(QCA)
minimize(d.partybans, outcome = "PB{1}", conditions = c("C", "F", "T", "V"), include = "?", dir.exp = c(1, "1;2", 2, 1), all.sol = TRUE)

From C1P1:

M1:    C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + T{2}*V{0} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} -> PB{1}

From C1P2:

M1:    C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{2}*T{2}*V{0} -> PB{1}

I was expected to see similar but I see very, very different solutions. I then show this to one colleague and he said to ask on this help list. Kindly ask you to explain why I get so different solutions.

Thank you so much,
Dmitri

Dear Dmitri,

I am currently at the American QCA conference in Los Angeles, to responding a bit slow.
If I remember correctly, the issue you are experiencing  is due to a bug that has been solved a long time ago in the main package QCA, and which is still present in the QCApro copy package of that old version.

This means that QCApro is practically obsolete. I am not sure if you prefer to produce all possible solutions or simply used the default minimal disjunctively in package QCApro, but given that package QCA also produces those my advice is to simply stop using that package. I have my doubts the current maintainer has the necessary skills to patch that error.

And this is not the only problem that plagues that package. A much more serious one is that it cannot always guarantee a solution.

Consider this example:

set.seed(12345)
pichart <- matrix(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 1825, prob = c(0.2, 0.8), replace = TRUE), ncol = 73)
QCApro::solveChart(pichart)
  
[1,]
[2,]
[3,]
[4,]
[5,]
[6,]
[7,]
[8,]

parts:
Dear Dimitri,

I am personally a big fan of Professor Dusa's work, particularly the QCA package and accompanying textbook. Many authors have discussed the importance of adopting QCA as an approach, not just a blunt instrument. It is my understanding that the parsimonious and conservative/complex solution types are analytical steps in calculating the intermediate solution and, while they should still be examined and considered, they are typically less desirable. Ragin summarises the common preference for the intermediate solution in Redesigning Social Inquiry (pg. 175) "In general, intermediate solutions are preferred because they are often the most interpretable. When limited diversity is substantial, complex solutions can be exceedingly intricate because little or no simplification occurs. Likewise, under these same conditions, parsimonious solutions can be unrealistically simple, due to the incorporation of many (easy and difficult) counterfactual combinations. Intermediate solutions strike a balance between parsimony and complexity, based on the substantive and theoretical knowledge of the investigator" (note I have added the bold here). Examining all three solutions in the context of this substantive and theoretical knowledge should not be overlooked. I encourage you to read Professor Dusa's article titled Critical Tension: Sufficiency and parsimony in QCA.

Kind Regards,
Alicia 

On Monday, March 20, 2023 at 8:37:16 PM UTC+10 Thiem Alrik wrote:

Dear Dimitri,

 

Adrian Dusa’s answer is complete non-sense.

 

The QCApro package has been developed because the QCA package contained some serious problematic features. In short, the QCA package suppresses many viable models – which QCApro doesn’t. That is why you see more / other models. QCApro standardly reveals all possible models to the researcher. How problematic the practice of model concealment is, see the meta analysis in Thiem et al (2020) and Baumgartner and Thiem (2017).

 

In addition, the QCA package standardly still offers conservative and intermediate solutions, which have long been shown to have extremely high error rates as compared to the parsimonious solution (see attached article Baumgartner_Thiem_2020). The QCApro documentation thus clearly says that you shouldn’t use conservative or intermediate solutions. These features are still only there because of method testing evaluations.

 

Thus, if you want to carry out serious configurational research, you should be extremely careful with QCA.

 

In any case, the much better option is to use Coincidence Analysis (CNA) or Combinational Regularity Analysis (CORA). Both methods considerably outperform QCA on correct inference rates and analytical sophistication. For more details, see the attached articles Baumgartner and Ambühl (2020, on CNA), Thiem et al. (2022; into to CORA), and Thiem (2022, QCA Handbook).

 

Best wishes

Alrik

To conclude, if you only need very simple examples (simple not in terms of number of conditions but in simple PI charts), and don’t need intermediate solutions, QCApro might do the job. But for serious applications I recommend dropping it and use the main package QCA.

 

All the best,

Adrian

Dear Professors,

I ask to forgive for my English language, and I hope you understand me.
In using a replication example I was wanting to be certain about my solutions and compare the results from both packages, by using the data called "d.partybans".

The complex solutions and the most parsiomonious solutions are the same, except for the intermediate solution that it is different and I don't know why.

I use this code:

library(QCApro)
data(d.partybans)
eQMC(d.partybans, outcome = "PB{1}", exo.facs = c("C", "F", "T", "V"), dir.exp = c(1, "1;2", 2, 1))

p.sol: C{0} + C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + T{2}*V{0}

M1:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*V{0}) => PB{1}
M2:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*T{0}) => PB{1}

p.sol: C{0} + C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + F{0}*T{2} + F{1}*V{0}

M1:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*V{0}) => PB{1}
M2:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*T{0}) => PB{1}


And then I compare this solutions with what I obtained from the other package QCA:

library(QCA)
minimize(d.partybans, outcome = "PB{1}", conditions = c("C", "F", "T", "V"), include = "?", dir.exp = c(1, "1;2", 2, 1), all.sol = TRUE)

From C1P1:

M1:    C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + T{2}*V{0} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} -> PB{1}

From C1P2:

M1:    C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{2}*T{2}*V{0} -> PB{1}
